title: Check yourself: judgement calls around custom exceptions

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, what is wrong with using an exception to end a loop or to report an ordinary outcome?

options.text: It is slower and harder to read than a return value or an Optional
options.says: The page lists it as a pitfall for exactly these reasons and keeps exceptions for exceptional conditions.

options.text: It is faster than an Optional, though a little harder to read
options.says: The page says the opposite about speed: an exception used this way is slower than a return value or an Optional.

options.text: It is fine once the exception class turns off its own stack trace
options.says: The page does not make an exception for cheap exceptions: an ordinary outcome belongs in a return value or an Optional.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: Per this page, which exceptions of a public method get a Javadoc `@throws` tag?

options.text: The checked ones, since the signature lists them anyway
options.says: The page asks for a tag on unchecked exceptions too, which the signature does not show.

options.text: Each one it can throw, whether checked or unchecked
options.says: The page's seventh key point: every exception a public method can throw, checked or unchecked, gets a @throws tag.

options.text: The unchecked ones, since the compiler ignores them
options.says: The page asks for tags on checked exceptions as well, not only on unchecked ones.

concepts: Every exception a public method can throw, checked or unchecked, gets a Javadoc @throws tag.
Exceptions are for exceptional conditions, not for ending a loop or signalling an ordinary outcome.
